transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood Solutions), Priya (CTO - Monolith), Gabe (Lead ML Eng), Sofia (Platform)
Recording: https://redwood-recordings/ff/2026-07-21-monolith (placeholder)
Agenda: token-level telemetry, OTLP integration, dashboards, KV-cache observability, batching windows, quantization impact, VPC/on-prem network considerations, next steps

Summary (auto): High-level alignment on instrumenting token-level metrics via OpenTelemetry, agreed to share sample prompts and run a benchmark. Discussed tradeoffs of client-side vs runtime-side token instrumentation, histogram bucketing for token latency, KV cache hit/miss metrics, and network egress considerations for VPC deployments.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone uh welcome thanks for making time today, I know we have a fair bit to get through so we can start with quick intros
[00:06] Priya Shah: yeah thanks, Priya from Monolith, we're the team that runs inference for our clinical NLP pipelines, trying to get better visibility into per-token costs and regressions
[00:12] Gabe Morales: Gabe here - leads machine learning infra, mainly focused on latency SLOs and model regressions
[00:17] Maya Chen: great, Ethan do you wanna set the technical agenda?
[00:19] Ethan Park: yeah thanks Maya, so we'll cover how Redwood emits token-level telemetry and integrates with OpenTelemetry, typical OTLP collector configs, dashboard patterns for token latency and KV cache observability, sampling/trace strategies, plus practical notes for VPC/private deployments and quantization effects you saw in your internal tests
[00:33] Sofia Lind: quick ask - we want to be able to correlate a token-level spike back to the prompt and to the model version, so looking for fields and trace ids we should add
[00:41] Luis Ortiz: perfect question - we'll show the field mapping, trace/span design, and the recommended labels for model_version, route_id, tenant_id, and prompt_hash (not raw prompt) to keep things privacy-friendly
[00:51] Priya Shah: noted, prompt_hash is fine, we do need to keep PHI out of logs though, so hashing is important
[00:57] Ethan Park: right, we don't send raw prompts by default. ok jumping in - here's how we instrument token-level events: Redwood runtime emits a token_event span for each token generation step. The span includes duration_ms, token_index, kv_cache_hit boolean, and a token_cost_estimate field. We batch-export spans over OTLP to your collector, you can back them into Datadog/AWS X-Ray/Splunk
[01:18] Gabe Morales: for high throughput that's a lot of spans - what's your recommended sampling?
[01:22] Ethan Park: two layers - first, continuous metrics (aggregated counters/histograms) are emitted at runtime so you get per-route token latency histograms and kv_cache hit-rate without needing to keep every span. Second, sample token_event spans at low rate (0.5% - 2%) for trace-level debugging. For P99 debugging we recommend targeted sampling on traces where the route latency exceeds a threshold - e.g., route_p95 > 300ms, then increase sampling on those routes for a period
[01:47] Priya Shah: can you explain the aggregated metric approach more, so we don't have to ingest millions of spans into our tracing backend?
[01:54] Luis Ortiz: sure. the runtime maintains per-request micro-aggregates during generation and emits aggregated metrics every 5s: token_count, token_latency_histogram (exponential buckets), kv_cache_hits, kv_cache_misses, batch_size_distribution. These are OTLP metrics that map to your metrics backend as histograms/counters. The histogram uses base-2 exponential buckets tuned for token latencies (1ms, 2ms, 4ms, 8ms... up to 2s)
[02:21] Gabe Morales: that bucket set seems reasonable for our median but what about tail behavior during cold KV cache misses?
[02:28] Ethan Park: cold KV cache misses can add 30-150ms depending on model size and remote storage. We recommend a separate gauge metric kv_remote_fetch_ms as part of aggregated emit. That allows you to break down token_latency_histogram into local_exec_ms vs kv_fetch_ms components
[02:44] Priya Shah: interesting, in our current setup we see spikes when the model's KV cache evaporates during autoscale events, is there an autoscale pattern to avoid that?
[02:53] Luis Ortiz: common pattern is warm-up prefetch on scale-up. Redwood Dedicated supports pre-warming KV caches by replaying top cached prefixes; you can schedule a short warm-up job post-scale. Also use a staggered scale policy so all replicas don't spin up simultaneously
[03:07] Sofia Lind: about dashboards - would you recommend token latency per-route or per-model dashboards?
[03:12] Ethan Park: both. per-route dashboards for SLAs and per-model for model-level regressions. We often build a composite dashboard: top panel for P50/P95/P99 token latency (histogram percentiles), middle for kv_cache_hit_rate by replica, bottom for batch_size distribution and cost per token. Also include an errors panel showing fallback events and model-variant swaps
[03:31] Gabe Morales: curious about correlating token spikes to prompts, you said prompt_hash - how do you recommend storing that in traces?
[03:38] Luis Ortiz: include prompt_hash and prompt_signature (structured, e.g., template id) as trace labels. For privacy, do not include full prompt text in traces unless required and encrypted at rest. If you need full prompt for debugging, use a secure artifact store with audit logging and link via short-lived reference id in the trace
[03:56] Priya Shah: that fits our compliance needs. now, VPC specifics - we run a private VPC deployment with HSM KMS. how does telemetry egress look in that configuration?
[04:05] Ethan Park: good one. In VPC/private mode we support a few patterns: 1) push OTLP to your collector inside the VPC (recommended), 2) push to a managed collector in Redwood via secure peering or private link (requires network setup), or 3) use an intermediary agent that forwards to your external backend. For HSM/KMS, keys are customer-managed and logs are stored within your region
[04:27] Sofia Lind: does pushing OTLP inside the VPC affect runtime latency? we're concerned collecting metrics could add overhead to the serving path
[04:34] Luis Ortiz: the runtime exports asynchronously. the main cost is CPU for serialization and network egress. we've measured typical overhead at <1% CPU for token-level aggregated metrics. If you decide to emit full token spans the overhead can be significant, that's why we recommend aggregation + low-rate span sampling
[04:50] Gabe Morales: we ran quantization tests (4-bit q4 vs 8-bit) and saw lower throughput but slightly higher token latency variance on q4 for some long sequences. what's the expectation on telemetry for quantized models?
[04:59] Ethan Park: quantization primarily changes compute latency per-token and memory profile. Telemetry-wise, you'll see a shift in token_latency_histogram and sometimes more variance due to kernel selection. We tag metrics with quant_profile like q4_0, q8_1 so you can filter dashboards. Also add a gauge for effective_throughput_rps to capture end-to-end throughput changes
[05:17] Priya Shah: about batching windows - we need to balance P95 latency vs cost, any heuristics?
[05:22] Luis Ortiz: common heuristic: use dynamic batching with a short max-latency window (e.g., 8-12ms) for low-latency routes and larger windows for high-throughput background routes (50-100ms). The runtime chooses kernels based on effective batch size; add a metric batch_wait_ms and batch_effective_tokens to tune the window.
[05:38] Gabe Morales: do you do continuous A/B for batching policies?
[05:41] Ethan Park: yes we support rollout policies per-route. You can canary a batching policy for a slice of traffic, measure token latency histograms and cost per token, and then roll forward. Redwood Optimize can suggest windows based on historical token arrival distributions
[05:56] Priya Shah: any gotchas with OTLP collector endpoints behind private subnets?
[06:01] Luis Ortiz: ensure collector endpoints are reachable from serving nodes. If collectors are in separate subnets ensure correct route tables and security groups. Also watch UDP/MTU fragmentation if you're using gRPC with larger payloads for compressed metrics; sometimes you need to tweak keepalive intervals and max_recv_message_size
[06:19] Sofia Lind: we use Datadog; how much cardinality are we looking at if we tag by route/model/tenant/prompt_signature? We worry about exploding series
[06:27] Ethan Park: good point, cardinality is the main truth-killer. Use route/model/tenant as high-cardinality but stable tags, avoid prompt_hash as metric label - keep prompt_hash only in traces. For metrics, aggregate by prompt_signature/template id which has limited cardinality. Also roll up by model_family when possible
[06:43] Gabe Morales: can you show an example OTLP mapping or sample span?
[06:46] Luis Ortiz: yeah I'll paste that in follow-up but example token_event span fields: span.name = token.generate, attributes: model_version, route_id, tenant_id, token_index, duration_ms, kv_cache_hit, token_cost_estimate, prompt_signature, trace_id, sample_rate. Batch-level metric emit has metric names: redwood.token.latency_histogram, redwood.kv.hits, redwood.kv.fetch_ms, redwood.batch.size_distribution
[07:09] Maya Chen: I'll stop sharing here but Ethan can drop the OTLP YAML after the call.
[07:14] Ethan Park: quick question for you Gabe - what are your current SLO targets for P99 and P95?
[07:18] Gabe Morales: P95 for interactive features is 350ms, P99 is 700ms, but for batch jobs it's looser. Our pain is sudden regressions in P99 after model updates
[07:26] Ethan Park: okay for regressions, we recommend a regression alerting pipeline: baseline token histograms for a stable prompt set (our eval harness), compare new model version histograms with KS-test or percentile diffs, alert on >10% P99 regressions. We can provide the eval harness integration as part of Optimize
[07:44] Priya Shah: that aligns with our expectations. Now, a tricky area - correlating trace-level events back to storage IO (S3 pulls for model shards) during cold starts. How do you instrument that?
[07:54] Luis Ortiz: we instrument storage fetches as separate spans: shard_fetch.start and shard_fetch.end with attributes bytes_fetched and storage_latency_ms and storage_backend. Then in dashboards you can create composite views that stack token_latency histogram and shard_fetch latency series to see correlation during scale events
08:12 Gabe Morales: I'm concerned about the extra tagging we might need; will that increase storage costs in our metrics backend?
08:17 Ethan Park: more tags -> more series. We recommend metrics tiering: high-cardinality traces stored at short retention and aggregated histograms stored at longer retention. Many customers keep full traces for 7-14 days and metric histograms for 90+ days
08:29 Sofia Lind: what's a realistic ingestion rate for aggregated metrics for a 500 RPS workload across 4 replicas?
08:34 Luis Ortiz: rough calc: aggregated emits every 5s per replica per route. If you have 10 routes that's (4 replicas * 10 routes * (60/5)) = 480 metric emits per minute ~ 8 per second. Each emit contains ~6 metrics, so ~48 metrics/sec - small. Spans are the heavy part if you emit raw token spans
08:55 Priya Shah: ok good, that seems fine. now can we talk about sampling strategies for debugging tail-latency? you mentioned targeted sampling earlier
09:03 Ethan Park: targeted sampling works like this: runtime checks a simple rule engine per request - if request_latency > X or kv_cache_miss_rate > Y or model_variant_fallback true, then increase span sampling for that route to 20-50% for a short window and emit a high-detail trace. Otherwise keep low-base sampling 0.5%
09:22 Gabe Morales: do you support tracing context propagation if we call out to downstream services? we have enrichment steps that call internal PKG services for metadata
09:28 Luis Ortiz: yes we propagate W3C tracecontext across downstream calls. For private deployments we include instructions to wire up your internal collectors so you can stitch traces across services
09:36 Priya Shah: another compliance question: audit logs for who accessed traces and full prompts if we enable them?
09:41 Maya Chen: in Private mode you can keep artifact store in your account with KMS and audit logs. Redwood's control plane will still show access events, and we can enable RBAC controls so only certain users can request full prompt dumps
09:52 Gabe Morales: performance question - we see high variance when switching quant profiles on the fly. Can you suggest rollout best practices?
09:58 Ethan Park: avoid in-place quant profile flips on high-traffic routes. Instead create a model-variant (q8_1, q4_0), canary traffic slice, monitor token histograms and error rates, then promote. If you must migrate in place, do it during low-traffic windows and pre-warm KV caches
10:17 Sofia Lind: a small networking nit - gRPC keepalive settings? we had idle connections being killed and then cold start hits
10:22 Luis Ortiz: set long-enough keepalive for idle channels, and enable connection pooling on your collector. Also set reconnect backoff jitter parameters to avoid thundering herd on reconnect
10:31 Gabe Morales: could you outline what you'd like us to share for the perf benchmark?
10:34 Ethan Park: ideally 1k representative prompts that exercise short and long contexts, a traffic mix (ratio of interactive vs batch), expected P95/P99 targets, and whether you want quant profiles in test. We'll run against a dedicated test pool and provide token-level histograms and a CSV summary.
10:50 Priya Shah: sounds good. on the security front, are there any restrictions on telemetry fields for HIPAA compliance?
10:55 Maya Chen: avoid PHI in telemetry. We recommend prompt hashing, do not include patient identifiers or raw text. For HIPAA customers, use Private deployment with customer KMS and store artifact prompts only in encrypted S3 with strict IAM and audit trails
11:06 Gabe Morales: minor: do you support pushing metrics to Prometheus directly or via pushgateway?
11:09 Luis Ortiz: Redwood can emit OTLP metrics which you can convert to Prometheus via an OTLP -> Prometheus gateway in your VPC. We don't recommend exposing Prometheus scraping directly to runtime nodes due to scale and cardinality concerns
11:20 Sofia Lind: we'll need concrete dashboards - could you share a starter Grafana dashboard?
11:23 Ethan Park: yes we'll attach a starter Grafana JSON and a Datadog dashboard in the follow-up. It will include token latency percentiles, kv cache hit rate, batch wait distribution, quant_profile filter, and a panel to correlate shard_fetch latency
11:36 Priya Shah: one last question - do you provide any guidance on cost allocation per-tenant using token-level metrics?
11:40 Maya Chen: yes we emit token_count and token_cost_estimate per-aggregated emit. You can sum token_cost_estimate by tenant over billing windows. For strict cost allocation use dedicated capacity per tenant or labels that match your billing dimensions
11:54 Gabe Morales: ok that's helpful. want to recap next steps?
11:57 Maya Chen: recap: Ethan shares OTLP mapping, Grafana/Datadog starter dashboards, and benchmark run plan. Monolith shares prompts and SLO targets. Maya to share Dedicated pricing as an option. We'll schedule benchmark week of 2026-07-27.
12:11 Priya Shah: thanks all, appreciate the detail.
12:13 Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts and a short doc.
12:16 [END]
